line: Ten minutes, goblin. I am checking on you. Something should be on fire by now.
note: §2.2 clock pressure: the Overlord's whispers check in at the 10-minute mark; arson is the objective that can't be hidden.

line: Five minutes. What still stands lies {dir} — follow the smoke and stop admiring the pigs.
note: §2.2: at 5 the whisper names a direction; wayfinding is environmental (§2.8). Register from §2.10 — mockery over mourning.

line: Two minutes. The stones are {dir}. Run, thief — I close the portal, not the door.
note: §2.2: inside the final 2 the Overlord points you there outright; the runic site is the one safe tile and the extraction point (§2.1).

line: Their whole winter, stacked in one shed — light it and go. The guards are thickest here; that is the tax.
note: Sibling of the windmill Stage-1 bark: first-time prompt naming the objective, the payoff and the cost. Granary sits in the village core where guards are thickest (§2.8), a compact blaze (§2.1).

line: One torch in the wheat, goblin. The fire walks the rows itself — let their buckets try to keep up.
note: Sibling first-time prompt: field fire spreads row to row, the most visible arson and hardest to douse (§2.8); the town answers with bucket lines at the well (§2.6).

line: The first sack crosses the stones. It is mine now. No bell un-takes it.
note: Loot banks permanently the instant it physically reaches the runic site — wipe-proof (§1, §2.2).

line: Behold — a pig. Stolen from a hamlet too small for them to have named it. Tremble, Groatsworth.
note: Apocalyptic gravitas applied to petty theft; stolen livestock is loot-kind and banks at the stones (§2.9, §2.10, §1).

line: Their strongbox, emptied through its own smashed lid. They will blame the badger for that too.
note: Strongbox is a market-core destructible smashed open for its coins (§2.7, §3.2), and the town's first reaction is denial (§2.10).

line: A living witness, roped and delivered. Let him describe the badger to his king.
note: Prisoners bank as loot the instant the chain reaches the stones; the tribute the Overlord wants is captives, not a body count (§2.6, §2.7, §2.10).

line: Five of them in my circle now. Their little routines are going quiet. Bring me more proof they remember us.
note: §2.10: the denial visibly strains as the evidence piles up — one missing villager is a badger, a hamlet's worth is the punchline.

line: Not one soul left in that hamlet. Alive, every one. Let the county explain THAT with a badger.
note: "None Left Behind" +40 — every civilian marched home alive (§2.9); the joke's punchline finally landing on the people telling it (§2.10).

line: You brought me a rope chain, not a corpse pile. Proof they remember us. …adequate.
note: §2.10 explicitly asks for a distinct verdict flavor when the raid comes home with prisoners — "Bring me proof they remember us. …adequate."

line: Gold, a pig, three fires — and no one alive to say who took them. Adequate. I have seen rats do better. …adequate.
note: The "merely rich" verdict §2.10 contrasts against the capture-heavy one; the rats crack is the established register (§2.1).

line: Five lives spent for a quarter of your deeds. What reached the stones is mine. You, apparently, are not.
note: Loss by spending all 5 lives keeps only 25% of unbanked deeds; loot already at the stones or the Warren is safe regardless (§2.2, §1, §2.6).
